item.title: Aluminum heads for surplus in 2027 as supply shock fades
item.description: Aluminium is expected to swing into a surplus in 2027, potentially of more than 1 million metric tons, as analysts eye a wave of new supply from Indonesia a
item.dc:creator: Mining.com
item.content:encoded: Aluminium is expected to swing into a surplus in 2027, potentially of more than 1 million metric tons, as analysts eye a wave of new supply from Indonesia and a recovery in flows from Gulf smelters. Expectations for a supply bump have already helped push prices of the metal used in transport and packaging below $3,000 a ton this week to their lowest since December, after they hit four-year highs in June on trade disruptions from the Iran war and dwindling inventories. “We expect a substantial rebound in Middle East supply, with output rising to 6.4 million tons from 4.8 million tons this year,” Ross Strachan, head of aluminium raw materials at CRU, said. The Middle East, which accounts for around 9% of global primary aluminium capacity, has seen shipments severely disrupted by the Iran war. CRU sees a 1.4 million-ton surplus next year, compared to a deficit of 711,000 tons this year. The world produced 73.8 million tons of primary aluminum in 2025. In Indonesia, where projects led by Chinese investors — unable to expand in their home market due to a capacity ceiling — are ramping up, CRU expects output to more than double from this year to 3.2 million tons in 2027. Growing pains Other analysts assume lower surpluses, cautioning that extra supply will be hard-won. Uday Patel, senior research manager at Wood Mackenzie, projects oversupply of around 500,000 tons next year against a 900,000-ton deficit this year. Gulf smelters are recovering but have been forced to use alternative routes to get their metal to export markets, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz at great expense. “You could see a situation where you have a surplus but still elevated premiums and potentially prices,” Patel said. He sees around 1 million tons of additional production from Indonesia next year but points to “growing pains” in the country’s aluminium sector. “The smelters are being built quicker than the infrastructure,” he said, with ports and power supply struggling to keep up. Bank of America commodity strategist Michael Widmer notes that the market had previously expected Indonesia to produce more than 2 million tons of aluminium this year, whereas the actual number could be closer to 1.2 million tons. “It’s coming, but slower than people thought,” said Widmer, who estimates 2.2 million tons of Indonesian supply next year — most of it in the second half — and a smaller surplus of 239,000 tons. (Reporting by Tom Daly; Editing by Jan Harvey)

item.title: U.S. Treasury Department’s investigation does not signal reduced bond issuance; U.S. Treasury yields rise as 10-year reclaims 5.12%
item.description: In a survey soliciting opinions from primary dealers, the Treasury Department asked about plans for repurchasing long-term government bonds, ways to enhance repo efficiency, the timing of short-term bond issuance, and prospects for the economy and financing, but did not directly address the issue of reducing long-term bond supply. Some investors had expected the Treasury to use this questionnaire to more clearly signal that it is considering scaling back the size of long-term bond auctions or even stopping the issuance of 20-year bonds, in response to the Trump administration's efforts to lower financing costs. The refinancing announcement to be released by the Treasury on November 4 has become the next observation point.
item.dc:creator: 华尔街见闻
item.content:encoded: The latest primary dealer survey by the U.S. Treasury did not provide a clear signal that it will imminently cut the size of long-term Treasury auctions, disappointing investors who were betting on government action to suppress long-term interest rates. As a result, U.S. Treasuries fell and yields generally rose. This survey is part of the Treasury's preparation for the quarterly refunding plan to be announced on November 4. The market had hoped to find clues from the questionnaire about whether Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen might adjust the size of long-term Treasury issuance, especially the much-discussed possibility of reducing or even halting the issuance of 20-year bonds. However, the Treasury only broadly asked what auction scale adjustments should be considered in the future, without explicitly suggesting that a supply cut for long-term debt is imminent. After the release of the Treasury's survey, U.S. Treasury yields rose across the board in the secondary market. The U.S. 10-year benchmark Treasury yield climbed back to 5.12%, approaching the day's pre-market high of 5.1315%, with the intraday gain expanding again to 6.5 basis points; the 20-year Treasury yield rose 5.4 basis points on the day, and the 30-year yield saw its intraday increase expand again to about 5 basis points. The 2-year yield erased its intraday decline and turned higher. Meanwhile, oil prices had already begun rising shortly before the survey was released, also adding upward pressure to U.S. Treasury yields. Therefore, Friday's yield rise reflected both disappointment that the Treasury failed to deliver a supply-reduction signal and the influence of changes in energy prices. What Did the Treasury Ask, and What Is the Market Waiting For? This time, the Treasury solicited opinions from primary dealers, focusing on what adjustments to Treasury auction sizes should be considered in the face of structural changes in investor demand, and with the expectation that medium-term demand may continue to evolve in the future. Such surveys are routine preparatory work for the Treasury’s quarterly refunding decisions, aimed at understanding the main dealers' assessments of government financing needs, investor demand, and market conditions, to inform the final determination of Treasury issuance scale and structure. The survey itself is not a funding plan, nor does it mean the Treasury has decided to adjust issuance sizes for any maturities. According to reports, this questionnaire also covered multiple debt management topics: Long-term Treasury Buyback Program: The Treasury asked whether expanding the size of long-term Treasury buybacks has improved market liquidity and trading operations; how larger buybacks would affect dealers' ability to fulfill client orders, and clients’ willingness to participate directly or indirectly in buybacks. Further Improving Buyback Efficiency: The Treasury solicited suggestions from dealers on what further adjustments could be made to the buyback program. T-Bills and Floating Rate Note Issuance Timing: The Treasury asked whether it should change the current practice of avoiding issuing T-bills and floating rate notes on FOMC rate decision days. Economic and Financing Outlook: Dealers also need to provide forecasts regarding the economy, fiscal and monetary policy, and the Treasury’s borrowing needs for the coming fiscal years. What really disappointed the market was that the Treasury did not directly address the issue of reducing long-term Treasury supply. Some investors had hoped that the Treasury would use this questionnaire to more clearly signal it is considering downsizing long-term bond auctions, or even halting 20-year bond issuance, in response to efforts (advocated by the Trump administration) to lower financing costs. Blake Gwinn, Head of U.S. Rates Strategy at RBC Capital Markets, said if the Treasury intended to send a signal or influence yields via the survey, it could have asked much more direct questions. He believes this survey conveyed no substantial signals; given that some investors expected significant adjustments such as discontinuing the 20-year bond, the outcome may have disappointed the market. 20-Year Bond in Focus, Wall Street Bets on Treasury Adjusting Issuance Structure The market is extremely sensitive to this survey, mainly because long-term Treasury yields have been high recently. With the persistent U.S. fiscal deficit and growing interest payments on existing debt, government financing needs are on the rise. Pressure from long-term Treasury supply has become a core concern for investors. According to Bloomberg, some Wall Street institutions previously bet that the Treasury might ease long-term bond supply pressure by adjusting issuance structure. The focus of discussion has especially been on the 20-year bond: whether the Treasury would cut its issuance size or even abolish this maturity outright. From a financing mechanism perspective, the Treasury must meet the government's overall borrowing needs but does not have to issue each maturity type in fixed proportions. If there is sufficient demand and market capacity for short-term instruments, in theory, the Treasury could boost short-term debt issuance and thus reduce supply pressures in the long-term bond market. However, adjusting maturity structure also changes the government’s future refinancing needs and cannot simply be interpreted as reducing total borrowing. Molly Brooks, U.S. Rates Strategist at TD Securities, said the Treasury’s questions are still too general and do not explicitly ask whether to reduce long-term bond supply, hence the disappointment in the market. She expects any adjustment to long-term bond auction sizes is unlikely before February 2027 at the earliest. This means the optimistic scenario that some investors had bet on—where the Treasury would announce cuts to long-term issuance, or even eliminate the 20-year bond, in the November quarterly refunding plan—may not materialize soon. The questionnaire did not provide a clear supply-reduction signal, nor does it rule out potential future adjustments. Issuance Signal Disappoints, Oil Price Surge Adds to Long-End Yield Pressure Beyond the Treasury’s survey, rising oil prices have also added upward pressure on Treasury yields. Higher energy prices could reignite inflation concerns and affect investors’ views of the future path of Fed interest rates. For longer-dated Treasuries, inflation expectations, future short-term rates, and required term premiums all influence yield pricing. This also explains why the market reaction was concentrated in long-dated Treasuries. Long-term bond prices are especially sensitive to changes in supply expectations: if investors were expecting the Treasury to reduce long-end issuance and such signals are missing, they may reassess both the amount of long-term bonds they must hold and the returns they demand for taking on interest rate risk. However, it would be wrong to attribute Friday’s rise in yields solely to the Treasury survey. Changes in oil prices were also highlighted as a driver in reports; the survey results merely fell short of the market’s hopes for a more proactive policy shift, and do not directly prove that the scale of future long-term Treasury issuance will remain unchanged. November 4 Refund Announcement Becomes the Next Focal Point The Treasury will announce the next quarterly refunding plan on November 4, at which point the market will be able to further assess the government's views on borrowing needs, issuance sizes for different maturities, and the specifics of buyback arrangements. The U.S. government faces persistent budget deficits, and interest on existing debt is also rising, which means the Treasury must strike a balance among financing costs, market demand, and the maturity structure of debt. Cutting long-term supply to lower long-end yields is one possible path the market is watching, but it is not without constraints. Before the formal announcement, dealer surveys are only market consultations and not policy commitments. The drop in long-end Treasury prices and renewed rise in yields on Friday reflected that the market was originally hoping for a more proactive supply-reduction signal from the Treasury, which was not sufficiently evident in the survey. Going forward, investors will continue to watch whether the Treasury adjusts its long-end issuance plans in the November refunding, and whether such moves can truly alleviate the supply pressure on long-term Treasuries.
